meta.title: SYNGAP1: From Brain to Atom
meta.description: An interactive explainer that traces SYNGAP1-Related Disorder from the whole brain down to the chemical elements it is built from, with plain-language facts and real published research at every level.
meta.disclaimer: This app is an educational summary compiled from published scientific and medical literature. It is not medical advice. Research is evolving quickly — always check with a physician or genetic counselor for guidance specific to an individual, and consult the original sources for the most current findings. The 3D models in this app are stylized, schematic visualizations built to teach concepts and relative proportions — they are not photorealistic anatomy, true atomic-scale structures, or the literal solved 3D fold of SYNGAP1.

levels.name: The Brain
levels.tagline: Where SYNGAP1-Related Disorder is seen and diagnosed
levels.summary: SYNGAP1-Related Disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by changes in a single copy of the SYNGAP1 gene on chromosome 6. Nearly all cases arise new in the child (de novo) rather than being inherited. Because the disorder affects how synapses mature and how brain circuits wire up during development, its effects show up across intellectual, motor, sensory, and behavioral domains — not in one isolated area.
facts: Caused by de novo (new, non-inherited) pathogenic variants in one copy of the SYNGAP1 gene on chromosome 6p21.32
Mechanism is haploinsufficiency: one working gene copy makes too little SynGAP protein for typical brain development
Intellectual disability occurs in essentially all affected individuals, typically moderate to severe
Epilepsy develops in roughly 65-85% of patients, often between 6 months and 7 years of age
Brain MRI is usually structurally normal — this is a disorder of synaptic wiring and timing, not visible brain malformation

sections.heading: What is SYNGAP1-Related Disorder?
sections.text: SYNGAP1-Related Disorder (SYNGAP1-RD, also called SYNGAP1-related intellectual disability, historically 'MRD5') is caused by pathogenic variants in the SYNGAP1 gene, which provides instructions for a protein critical at the synapse — the junction where brain cells communicate. When one copy of the gene is broken or missing, the body can't produce enough of this protein, a mechanism called haploinsufficiency. This disrupts how synapses mature and how neural circuits form during early brain development.

sections.heading: How common is it?
sections.text: Estimates vary depending on how the condition is counted. Framed as a rare disease, SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy is estimated to affect fewer than 1 in 1,000,000 people, and global patient registries have identified roughly 1,800+ confirmed cases worldwide — a floor, since it only counts people who have had genetic testing and registered. Framed instead as a cause of intellectual disability, SYNGAP1 variants are found in about 0.75% of children with intellectual disability in large sequencing cohorts and roughly 1% of people with epileptic encephalopathy — making it one of the more frequently identified single-gene causes once broad genetic testing (exome/genome sequencing) is performed.

sections.heading: Core clinical effects
sections.text: Intellectual disability occurs in essentially all affected individuals, typically moderate to severe, with about one-third remaining nonverbal. Epilepsy develops in a majority of patients with a fairly distinctive seizure profile: eyelid myoclonia with absences, myoclonic and myoclonic-atonic seizures ('drop attacks'), atypical absences, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, sometimes triggered by eating. About half of patients respond to a single anti-seizure medication; the rest are drug-resistant. Autism spectrum features appear in roughly half of individuals. Early hypotonia (low muscle tone) is nearly universal in infancy, walking is typically delayed to around 26 months, and many children develop an unsteady, ataxic gait. Sleep difficulties, an elevated pain threshold, sound sensitivity (hyperacusis), and behavioral challenges such as inattention and self-injurious behavior are also commonly reported.

sections.heading: The state of research
sections.text: Research interest has grown substantially since SYNGAP1 was first linked to intellectual disability in 2009, accelerating over the past decade as genetic sequencing became routine. Patient organizations such as CURE SYNGAP1 (formerly SynGAP Research Fund) fund research, run natural-history patient registries, and have committed over $8 million to research partners. Current therapeutic development is moving toward gene- and RNA-based approaches aimed at restoring SYNGAP1 protein levels rather than only managing symptoms. In July 2026, CAMP4 Therapeutics received Australian regulatory clearance to begin a first-in-human trial of CMP-002, an RNA-targeting (antisense oligonucleotide) therapy designed to increase SYNGAP1 gene expression, while other groups are separately pursuing AAV-based gene-therapy strategies.

levels.laymanTagline: The complete global shipping network — where SYNGAP1-RD shows up
levels.laymanSummary: Think of the brain as a worldwide shipping network that moves 'packages' (messages) everywhere the body needs them, nonstop. SYNGAP1-Related Disorder is caused by a change in one copy of a gene called SYNGAP1 — it's not something a child catches, and it's not something a parent did, almost always a brand-new, one-time change. Because this gene helps the network's routes and stations grow and connect correctly, its effects can touch many parts of life: learning, movement, communication, and behavior.
laymanFacts: It's caused by a change in one copy of the SYNGAP1 gene — almost always a brand-new change, not something passed down from a parent.
It affects learning and thinking in nearly everyone diagnosed, usually in the moderate-to-severe range.
Seizures happen in most children with SYNGAP1-RD, often starting somewhere between infancy and age 7 — like a surge that overwhelms the whole network at once.
A brain MRI or scan usually looks normal — the differences are in how the network runs, not in how the buildings and roads look from the outside.
levels.laymanCaption: The complete global shipping network that moves packages worldwide.

levels.name: Brain Regions
levels.tagline: The hippocampus and cortex are where SYNGAP1 research concentrates
levels.summary: Within the brain, SYNGAP1 research concentrates heavily on two regions: the hippocampus, the brain's memory-formation hub, and the neocortex, especially layer 2/3, which integrates sensory and cognitive information. Notably, structural brain scans (MRI) in people with SYNGAP1-RD are usually normal — the disorder shows up in how circuits function and wire together, not in visible brain structure.
facts: The hippocampus is the most-studied region because it drives memory formation and is the classic model for long-term potentiation (LTP)
Syngap1 heterozygous mice show roughly 45-50% weaker LTP at the hippocampal CA3-to-CA1 synapse, tracking with spatial memory deficits
Neocortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons show premature dendritic spine and synapse maturation, shortening a normal developmental 'critical period'
Loss of SynGAP specifically in inhibitory interneurons in sensory cortex impairs the brain's ability to filter irrelevant sensory input
Structural brain MRI is typically normal or nonspecific despite substantial functional impact — 'normal scan, abnormal function'

sections.heading: Hippocampus: the memory hub
sections.text: The hippocampus is the single most-studied region in SYNGAP1 research because it is the brain's core hub for forming new memories and for long-term potentiation (LTP) — the leading laboratory model of how learning physically strengthens synapses. Because SynGAP protein is highly enriched at excitatory synapses in hippocampal neurons, most foundational mouse studies record electrical activity directly from hippocampal brain slices, especially the CA3-to-CA1 synapse. Syngap1 heterozygous mice show roughly 45-50% weaker LTP at this synapse, which tracks closely with deficits on hippocampus-dependent spatial memory tasks like the Morris water maze — giving researchers a direct physical link between a single gene, a specific synapse, and a measurable memory problem.

sections.heading: Neocortex: sensory and cognitive integration
sections.text: SynGAP is also highly expressed in the cortex, and layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons — cells central to relaying and integrating sensory and cognitive information — mature abnormally when SynGAP is reduced. Studies find 'precocious' (too-early) dendritic spine and synapse maturation in cortical pyramidal cells, shortening a normal developmental critical period during which circuits are supposed to stay flexible and fine-tune themselves. This may help explain why SYNGAP1-RD involves broad cognitive impairment rather than damage confined to one skill. When SynGAP is lost specifically from inhibitory (GABAergic) interneurons in sensory cortex, neurons lose their ability to filter out irrelevant sensory information and animals struggle to learn sensory-discrimination tasks — a plausible circuit-level explanation for sensory processing difficulties in SYNGAP1-RD.

sections.heading: Other regions and human imaging
sections.text: The cerebellum is not a major focus of SYNGAP1 research, though SynGAP protein is expressed there during development. Thalamus, primary sensory cortex circuits, and anterior cingulate cortex have also been studied in mouse models, tied to sensory dysregulation and behavior. Notably, structural brain MRI in people with SYNGAP1-RD is typically reported as normal or without a consistent, distinctive abnormality, despite significant intellectual disability, epilepsy, and autism features. This 'normal scan, abnormal function' pattern supports the conclusion from animal models that SYNGAP1-RD is primarily a disease of synaptic wiring and timing rather than gross structural brain malformation.

levels.laymanTagline: Major cities in the network, each with its own specialty
levels.laymanSummary: Just like New York and Tokyo each play a different role in a shipping network, different brain regions specialize in different jobs. Researchers focus closely on two of these 'cities': the hippocampus, which handles memory, and the cortex, which handles thinking and the senses. Even though the cities' skylines (brain scans) usually look normal from the outside, they don't run quite the same way in someone with SYNGAP1-RD.
laymanFacts: The hippocampus is like the network's memory-storage city — it's one of the most-studied areas in SYNGAP1 research.
The cortex, the 'thinking city,' processes things a bit too fast and too early, which can shortcut normal learning.
Even the city that filters incoming sights, sounds, and touch can get overloaded, making some input feel overwhelming.
A brain scan (MRI) almost always looks normal — the changes are too small to see in a photo of the skyline, only in how the city actually runs.
levels.laymanCaption: Separate major cities in the network like New York or Tokyo that handle specific jobs.

levels.name: Neural Circuits
levels.tagline: Excitation and inhibition fall out of balance
levels.summary: Every brain circuit runs on a balance between excitatory signals (which push neurons to fire) and inhibitory signals (which restrain firing). SYNGAP1 loss tips this excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance toward excess excitation, producing measurable network hyperexcitability that is linked to seizures, and disrupting the developmental timing that lets circuits refine themselves through experience.
facts: E/I balance keeps neural networks stable and paces 'critical periods' when circuits are especially moldable by experience
SynGAP normally restrains how fast excitatory synapses mature; without it, circuits 'lock in' before experience has shaped them
SynGAP is also expressed in inhibitory interneurons, where it helps regulate their synaptic drive and excitability
Mouse models show elevated EEG power, more frequent electrographic spikes, and abnormal bursting — the electrophysiological signature of seizure-prone circuits
In somatosensory cortex, altered E/I balance degrades sensory information coding, linking circuit disruption to sensory processing differences, not just seizures

sections.heading: What is excitation/inhibition balance?
sections.text: Every brain circuit runs on a balance between excitatory signals (which push neurons to fire, mainly via glutamate) and inhibitory signals (which restrain firing, mainly via GABA-releasing interneurons). This E/I balance keeps neural networks active enough to process information but not so active that activity runs away uncontrolled. It also sets the pace of 'critical periods' — developmental windows when circuits are especially moldable by experience. When balance tips toward excess excitation or insufficient inhibition, the result can range from subtle circuit noise to seizures.

sections.heading: How SYNGAP1 loss disrupts the balance
sections.text: SynGAP normally acts as a brake on excitatory synapses, restraining how fast they mature and how many receptors they accumulate. With only one working copy of SYNGAP1, this brake is weakened: excitatory synapses mature too fast and accumulate excess receptors ahead of schedule. In mouse cortex, this causes critical periods of synaptic plasticity to close prematurely — the circuit 'locks in' before experience has had normal time to shape it. SynGAP is also expressed in inhibitory interneurons themselves, where it helps regulate their synaptic drive; reducing SynGAP there impairs inhibitory synapse formation and function. The E/I imbalance in SYNGAP1-RD appears to come from at least two directions: excess, premature excitatory drive and compromised inhibitory circuitry.

sections.heading: Hyperexcitability and seizures
sections.text: Multiple mouse-model studies find measurable network hyperexcitability: elevated EEG power, more frequent and longer electrographic spike events, and abnormal bursting patterns in cortical networks. This is consistent with excess excitation overwhelming inhibitory control, producing circuits prone to synchronized, runaway firing — the electrophysiological substrate of seizures. Human SYNGAP1-RD is associated with epilepsy in the large majority of patients. Beyond seizures, altered E/I balance disrupts how sensory circuits are built: in somatosensory cortex, SYNGAP1 heterozygous mice show reduced and abnormal touch-evoked neural activity and degraded sensory information coding, connecting circuit-level disruption directly to the sensory processing differences seen in SYNGAP1-RD, not only to seizures.

levels.laymanTagline: The highways that connect the cities fall out of balance
levels.laymanSummary: Cities need highways to move trucks between them — and a healthy highway system balances 'go' signals (green lights) with 'stop' signals (red lights and on-ramps that meter traffic). In SYNGAP1-RD, there's too much 'go' and not enough 'stop,' so the highways get overloaded. That's a big part of why seizures and sensory overload can happen.
laymanFacts: Think of it like a highway with too many on-ramps open at once and not enough traffic lights to meter the flow.
This imbalance can make the highway system 'finish construction' too quickly, before it's had a chance to be fine-tuned by everyday traffic patterns.
It's linked to seizures, because an overloaded highway can trigger a much bigger citywide traffic jam — an electrical 'storm.'
It can also make everyday sounds, lights, or textures feel like 'too much traffic,' because the network has a harder time filtering out what doesn't matter.
levels.laymanCaption: The major highway systems connecting the cities so trucks can travel.

levels.name: Neurons
levels.summary: Dendritic spines are tiny protrusions on neurons that house excitatory synapses. Spines normally mature slowly, letting a young brain sample many possible connections before settling on useful ones. SYNGAP1 loss causes spines to mature too early and too uniformly, denying neurons the normal window of 'trial and error' needed to build precisely tuned circuits.
facts: Dendritic spines are the receiving end of excitatory synapses; young spines are thin and motile, maturing over weeks into stable, mushroom-shaped structures
SynGAP normally restrains signaling that drives spine maturation; without it, spines thicken and stabilize prematurely
The damage happens in a defined early developmental window — restoring SynGAP in adulthood does not reverse the resulting cognitive deficits
The effect is selective for excitatory (glutamatergic) neurons; removing SynGAP only from inhibitory interneurons has no cognitive effect
Human iPSC-derived neurons with SYNGAP1 loss show the same accelerated maturation seen in mice: larger dendrites, more synapses, earlier and burstier activity

sections.heading: What dendritic spines are and why they matter
sections.text: Dendritic spines are tiny, mushroom- or thorn-shaped protrusions that stud the branches (dendrites) of excitatory neurons. Each mature spine houses one excitatory synapse — the postsynaptic density where signals from an upstream neuron are received and converted into electrical and biochemical changes. Spine shape is not static: young spines are long, thin, and motile, and normally mature slowly over weeks into stubby, stable structures as circuits refine through experience. This gradual maturation lets a young brain sample many possible connections before 'locking in' the useful ones.

sections.heading: SYNGAP1: a developmental brake on spine maturation
sections.text: SynGAP is highly concentrated at excitatory postsynaptic densities, where it normally restrains signaling that drives receptor insertion and spine enlargement. In Syngap1 haploinsufficient mice, this brake is weakened, and dendritic spines mature abnormally early, thickening and stabilizing prematurely instead of following the normal, protracted developmental timeline. This premature maturation produces hyperexcitable hippocampal circuits in juvenile mice, and the damage is done during a defined early developmental window: inducing the mutation later in life has little effect, and restoring SynGAP in adulthood does not reverse the cognitive deficits — establishing spine maturation timing itself as a critical determinant of later cognitive capacity.

sections.heading: Cell-type specificity and human confirmation
sections.text: The damage is selective for excitatory neurons: restricting Syngap1 haploinsufficiency to forebrain glutamatergic neurons is sufficient to cause cognitive deficits, while manipulating the gene only in inhibitory interneurons has no cognitive effect. Because spines mature too fast and too uniformly, individual neurons lose the normal period of synaptic 'trial and error' needed to build precisely tuned circuits, producing persistently enhanced excitatory synaptic strength that predicts cognitive impairment. Using human stem-cell-derived neurons with CRISPR-edited SYNGAP1 loss, researchers confirmed the same acceleration in human cells: neurons grew larger dendritic arbors, formed more excitatory synapses, and showed elevated, burstier network firing — showing the mouse findings translate to human neurobiology.

levels.laymanSummary: Neurons are the individual delivery trucks driving the highways, carrying messages from city to city. Normally, young trucks spend time testing out different routes before settling into their regular ones. In SYNGAP1-RD, the trucks lock into their final routes too quickly and too uniformly — skipping the normal trial-and-error period that shapes an efficient network.
laymanFacts: Each truck (neuron) has thousands of possible stops, and it's supposed to try out many of them slowly before settling on its regular route.
With SYNGAP1-RD, trucks lock onto their final route too early, so the network doesn't get its full 'trial run' period.
This happens during a specific, early window during construction — which is why researchers care so much about early diagnosis and intervention.
It shows up the same way in brain cells grown in a lab from people with SYNGAP1-RD, confirming this isn't just something seen in animal studies.
levels.laymanCaption: The individual delivery trucks driving down the highways to carry messages.

levels.name: Synapses
levels.tagline: SynGAP is a gatekeeper of synaptic strength
levels.summary: A synapse is the junction where neurons communicate. SynGAP is one of the most abundant proteins in the postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses, where it acts as a brake on signaling that inserts glutamate receptors into the synaptic membrane. This brake is what allows synapses to strengthen in a controlled, timed way during learning — and losing half of it leaves synapses wired too strong, too early.
facts: SynGAP is one of the most abundant proteins in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of excitatory synapses, at concentrations similar to the master scaffold protein PSD-95
It works by keeping Ras/Rap signaling low, restraining insertion of AMPA-type glutamate receptors into the synaptic membrane
During learning (long-term potentiation), calcium signaling causes SynGAP to briefly disperse from the spine, releasing the brake and allowing the synapse to strengthen
With only half the normal SynGAP, this brake is chronically weakened, causing excessive baseline receptor accumulation and premature spine maturation
SynGAP forms high-concentration, membraneless droplets with PSD-95 — a physical explanation for why the brain is so sensitive to SynGAP dosage

sections.heading: What is a synapse?
sections.text: A synapse is the junction where one neuron sends a chemical signal to the next. At excitatory synapses, the sending neuron releases the neurotransmitter glutamate, which binds receptors on the receiving neuron's dendritic spine. Just inside the receiving membrane sits the postsynaptic density (PSD) — a dense mesh of proteins that holds neurotransmitter receptors in place and decides, moment to moment, how strongly that synapse responds. The PSD is where synapses get physically and functionally tuned.

sections.heading: SynGAP's role at the synapse
sections.text: SynGAP is one of the most abundant proteins in the PSD of excitatory synapses — brain-specific, found essentially only in excitatory neurons. It encodes a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that normally acts as a brake, keeping Ras/Rap signaling low and restraining AMPA receptor insertion into the synaptic membrane, which keeps baseline synaptic strength in check. During long-term potentiation (the cellular basis of learning and memory), calcium influx activates an enzyme (CaMKII) that causes SynGAP to rapidly disperse out of the spine, releasing the brake. This lets Ras signaling drive receptor insertion and spine enlargement, strengthening the synapse in a controlled, transient window.

sections.heading: What happens with only half the protein
sections.text: With only about 50% of normal SynGAP, as in SYNGAP1-RD, this Ras/Rap brake is chronically weakened. This produces excessive baseline signaling and premature, excessive receptor accumulation at synapses, causing dendritic spines to mature too early and excitatory transmission to be abnormally elevated. It also shortens or shifts the normal critical period of synaptic plasticity during development. The net effect is synapses that are wired too strong, too early, and less able to undergo normal experience-dependent refinement — a proposed cellular mechanism underlying the intellectual disability, autism features, and epilepsy seen in SYNGAP1-RD.

levels.laymanTagline: The loading docks hand off packages too soon
levels.laymanSummary: A synapse is the loading dock where one truck's delivery gets handed off to the next leg of the journey. The SYNGAP1 protein normally works like a dock supervisor, making sure that handoff ramps up gradually and at the right pace as the network learns its routes. With only half the normal amount of this supervisor, the dock gets 'busy' and overloaded too soon.
laymanFacts: Think of a synapse as a loading dock — one truck drops a package off, and the next truck picks it up.
The SYNGAP1 protein is like the dock supervisor, keeping the handoff pace controlled instead of letting it get chaotic too fast.
With only half the usual amount of this protein, the supervisor is stretched too thin, so the dock gets overloaded before it should.
This is one of the most important discoveries in SYNGAP1 research — a hands-on explanation for why the network's timing gets thrown off.
levels.laymanCaption: The loading docks where trucks pass packages to the next station.

levels.name: The SYNGAP1 Protein
levels.tagline: A multi-domain molecular brake, 1,343 amino acids long

dnaLink.label: See how a DNA mutation breaks this protein →

levels.summary: SynGAP is a modular protein built from several folded domains, each with its own job: anchoring to the membrane, sensing calcium/lipids, and — most importantly — catalyzing a chemical reaction that turns off Ras/Rap signaling. The full-length protein is 1,343 amino acids long, encoded by the SYNGAP1 gene on chromosome 6, and mutations that disrupt any part of this structure can reduce its function.
facts: Full-length human SynGAP (isoform α1) is 1,343 amino acids, about 148 kDa, encoded by SYNGAP1 on chromosome 6p21.32
Its modular structure includes a PH domain, a C2 domain, a catalytic RasGAP domain, a coiled-coil region, and (in some isoforms) a PDZ-binding tail
The RasGAP domain contains an 'arginine finger' that speeds up GTP hydrolysis roughly 1,000-fold, turning off Ras/Rap signaling
Four isoforms (α1, α2, β, γ) differ mainly at the C-terminus, changing where and how strongly each version acts
Nonsense/frameshift variants typically eliminate functional protein; missense variants in the C2 or RasGAP domains distort the fold and cripple catalytic activity

sections.heading: What is a protein domain?
sections.text: A protein domain is a self-contained, folded section of a protein that acts like a functional module — similar to a Swiss Army knife with separate, purpose-built tools attached to one handle. Each domain folds into a specific 3D shape that lets it perform one job: gripping a membrane, binding a partner protein, or catalyzing a chemical reaction. If a domain's shape is disrupted, even by a change in one amino acid, it can lose its grip or catalytic ability, breaking the whole protein's function.

sections.heading: SynGAP's domain architecture
sections.text: SynGAP is built (from one end to the other) from a PH domain that helps anchor it to membranes; a C2 domain, a calcium/lipid-sensing fold that works with the PH domain to regulate access to the catalytic domain; a RasGAP domain, the catalytic core, which contains an 'arginine finger' that reaches into a bound Ras or Rap GTPase and speeds up its shutoff roughly 1,000-fold; a coiled-coil region that lets SynGAP molecules bind each other; and, in some isoforms, a short C-terminal tail that plugs into scaffold proteins like PSD-95, physically anchoring SynGAP inside the postsynaptic density.

sections.heading: Size, location, and core function
sections.text: The full-length human SynGAP protein is 1,343 amino acids, with a molecular weight of about 148 kDa. The SYNGAP1 gene is located on chromosome 6, band 6p21.32. Biochemically, SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP): small GTPases like Ras and Rap act as molecular on/off switches, and SynGAP's GAP domain dramatically speeds up their shutoff, restraining downstream signaling that controls receptor insertion at synapses.

sections.heading: Isoforms and how mutations cause disease
sections.text: Alternative splicing produces several isoforms — α1, α2, β, and γ — that differ mainly in their tail and differ in localization and signaling strength. SYNGAP1-RD is caused by haploinsufficiency: one gene copy carries a pathogenic variant, and the resulting reduced total SynGAP protein is insufficient for normal synaptic regulation. Nonsense and frameshift variants typically create premature stop codons leading to a broken or absent protein. Missense variants, especially in the C2 or RasGAP domains, distort the domain's fold or cripple its catalytic activity — again lowering effective SynGAP function even though the gene itself isn't entirely broken.

levels.laymanTagline: The dock worker who keeps the whole operation under control
levels.laymanSummary: The SYNGAP1 protein is the dock worker on site, built to do several jobs — anchoring equipment, sensing what's coming in, and, most importantly, hitting the brakes on the conveyor belt so packages don't pile up too fast. It's a big, multi-part worker: 1,343 amino acids long. When the gene that builds this worker is damaged, they can't slow the belt down properly.
laymanFacts: SYNGAP1 builds a dock worker whose main job is to hit the brakes on the conveyor belt, keeping packages from piling up too fast.
This worker carries several tools, but the most important one is the brake lever.
A change (mutation) in the gene can weaken or remove this worker's brake, depending on exactly where the change happens in their training.
This is why the condition is named after the gene — 'SYNGAP1-Related Disorder' literally means a disorder related to this dock worker.
levels.laymanCaption: The dock workers who build structures and move the packages.

levels.name: Amino Acids
levels.tagline: The 20 letters that spell out every protein

dnaLink.label: See how a DNA mutation changes an amino acid →

levels.summary: Amino acids are the building blocks that link together to form proteins, much like letters combine into words. The order of amino acids in SYNGAP1 — dictated by the gene's DNA sequence — determines how the protein folds into its working 3D shape. Changing even one amino acid at a critical position can break the whole protein's function.
facts: There are 20 standard amino acids, each sharing the same backbone but with a unique side chain (R-group) that gives it distinct chemistry
A protein's amino acid sequence ('primary structure') is dictated by the gene's DNA/mRNA codon sequence
The chemistry of each side chain causes the chain to fold into a precise 3D shape, creating functional pockets like SynGAP's catalytic site
Amino acids are grouped by side-chain chemistry: nonpolar/hydrophobic, polar/uncharged, charged (acidic/basic), and aromatic
A single amino acid substitution ('missense' change) in a compact catalytic domain like RasGAP can impair enzyme activity or destabilize the whole protein

sections.heading: What are amino acids?
sections.text: Amino acids are the small molecular building blocks that link together, end to end, to form proteins — much like letters combine to form words. There are 20 standard amino acids used by human cells. Every amino acid shares the same basic backbone (an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a central carbon), but each one has a unique side chain attached to that backbone, giving it a distinct size, shape, charge, and chemical behavior. A protein like SYNGAP1 is a specific, precisely ordered chain of hundreds of these amino acids.

sections.heading: From sequence to shape to function
sections.text: The order of amino acids in a protein is dictated by the sequence of codons in the gene — in this case, SYNGAP1. As the chain is assembled, the chemical properties of each amino acid's side chain cause it to bend, twist, and fold into a precise three-dimensional shape. This 3D shape creates functional pockets and surfaces, such as the catalytic site in SynGAP's RasGAP domain that acts on Ras/Rap signaling proteins. Function follows directly from shape, and shape follows directly from sequence.

sections.heading: Why one amino acid change can break the whole protein
sections.text: Because folding and function depend on the precise chemistry of each amino acid, swapping even a single one (a 'missense' change) at a critical position can be catastrophic — especially inside a compact catalytic domain like RasGAP, where a handful of residues must line up exactly to bind and act on their target. Research on SYNGAP1 missense variants has shown that substitutions in or near the GAP/C2 domains can impair enzymatic activity, destabilize the protein's fold, or disrupt its normal localization within neurons — all from changing just one 'letter' in a chain of over a thousand. This is the molecular logic behind many SYNGAP1-RD missense variants: the protein is rarely entirely 'gone' — more often, one wrong building block subtly or severely breaks its 3D machinery.

levels.laymanTagline: The LEGO bricks that snap together to build every worker
levels.laymanSummary: Dock workers (proteins) aren't hired ready-made — they're built, one small LEGO-like brick at a time. Amino acids are those bricks, snapping together in a specific order to build every worker in the network, including the SYNGAP1 dock worker. The exact order of bricks — spelled out by the gene's DNA blueprint — determines whether the finished worker can do their job.
laymanFacts: There are 20 different kinds of amino acid 'bricks' the body uses to build every protein worker.
The order they're snapped together in is set by the DNA blueprint in the gene — like an instruction booklet that spells out the exact build order.
Once snapped together, the brick chain folds up into a specific 3D shape — that shape is what lets the finished worker actually do their job.
Even swapping out just one brick in the wrong spot can keep the whole worker from being built correctly.

levels.name: Chemical Elements
levels.tagline: The atoms behind SYNGAP1 — and the whole brain
levels.summary: Every protein in the body, including SYNGAP1, is ultimately built from a handful of atom types: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and (in two amino acids) sulfur. These simple atoms bond into amino acids, which chain into the SYNGAP1 protein, which sits at synapses, which connect into neurons, which wire into circuits, which build the brain systems responsible for learning and cognition.
facts: Carbon (atomic number 6) forms four strong bonds at once, letting it build the long chains, branches, and rings needed for complex biological molecules
Hydrogen (atomic number 1) fills bonding spots and enables hydrogen bonding, the weak, reversible attractions that let proteins fold into precise shapes
Nitrogen (atomic number 7) forms the amino group (-NH2) that defines amino acids and the peptide bonds that link them into chains
Oxygen (atomic number 8) forms the carboxyl group (-COOH) and its high electronegativity drives protein folding and reactivity
Sulfur (atomic number 16), found in cysteine and methionine, can form disulfide bonds that act like molecular staples locking a protein's 3D shape in place

sections.heading: The five key elements
sections.text: Carbon (C, atomic number 6) is the backbone of life: each atom can form four strong bonds at once, letting it link into the long chains, branches, and rings needed for complex, stable biological shapes. Hydrogen (H, atomic number 1), the lightest and most abundant element, fills the remaining bonding spots on carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, and is central to hydrogen bonding — the weak attractions that let proteins fold into precise 3D shapes. Nitrogen (N, atomic number 7) forms three bonds and defines the 'amino' part of amino acid, the amino group (-NH2), and is essential to the peptide bonds that link amino acids into chains. Oxygen (O, atomic number 8) forms two bonds and appears in the carboxyl group (-COOH); its strong pull on shared electrons helps create the polarity that drives protein folding. Sulfur (S, atomic number 16) appears in only two of the twenty amino acids — cysteine and methionine — but its disulfide bonds act like molecular staples that lock a protein's 3D shape in place.

sections.heading: Why these elements build the molecules of life
sections.text: Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen are the most common elements in living things because they are light, abundant, and form strong yet adjustable covalent bonds. Carbon's four bonding sites give it structural versatility; nitrogen and oxygen contribute the reactive, polar chemical groups that give amino acids their distinctive 'front' and 'back' ends, allowing them to link head-to-tail into indefinitely long chains; hydrogen fills gaps and enables folding; sulfur adds extra structural locking where needed. Small differences in how these atoms are arranged create the twenty different amino acid building blocks used to build every protein, including SynGAP.

sections.heading: Zooming back out
sections.text: These simple atoms bond into amino acids. Amino acids link in a specific order — dictated by the SYNGAP1 gene — into a folded protein chain: the SYNGAP1 protein. That protein sits at synapses, the tiny junctions where neurons communicate, where it helps regulate signal strength as a brake on excitatory signaling. Synapses connect into neurons, neurons wire into circuits, and circuits form the brain systems responsible for learning, movement, and cognition. When SYNGAP1's amino acid sequence is altered by a genetic variant, the change can ripple all the way up — from atom, to protein, to synapse, to neuron, to circuit, to the whole brain — producing the features seen in SYNGAP1-Related Disorder.

levels.laymanTagline: The raw materials every brick is made from
levels.laymanSummary: Zoom in far enough, and every LEGO-like brick — and every worker, dock, truck, and city in the whole network — is molded from just a handful of raw materials: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur. These raw atoms combine into amino acid bricks, which snap together into the SYNGAP1 dock worker, who staffs the loading docks, which connect the trucks, which drive the highways, which link the cities that make up the whole shipping network — where SYNGAP1-RD shows up.
laymanFacts: Just five basic types of atoms — carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur — are molded into nearly every protein brick in the body, including SYNGAP1.
Carbon is the most important raw material — it can link to four other atoms at once, letting it form long chains and complex shapes, like a versatile molding material.
These atoms combine into amino acids, the 'bricks' from the level before this one.
It's the same handful of raw materials, all the way from a single molecule up to an entire, complex shipping network.
levels.laymanCaption: The raw carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms that form the bricks.
